The Sequencher project format

spf_format.Rd

Sequencher project files (.SPF) are undocumented. This page describes the parts of the format that read_spf() relies on, as worked out from a project saved by Sequencher 5.4 on a Mac. For the 150 reads in that project whose original .ab1 files survive, read_spf() reproduces the processed traces, peak positions and quality scores exactly. The 14 projects published with two studies (doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1006176 and Zenodo record 5557681) have no original files to compare against, but all 2,214 of their reads have one peak position per base, all within the trace, and the called base is the strongest trace channel at its peak for 94.8% of the 2.0 million A, C, G and T calls. Projects from other versions may differ.

Details

All integers are big-endian and all offsets are absolute byte positions in the file, counted from 0.

Overall layout

The file is a heap of tagged records and data blocks, with no table of contents at a fixed position. Records point at their data blocks by file offset, so the blocks for one read are scattered through the file and do not sit next to its record. Text such as read names, file paths, instrument names and annotation labels is stored null-terminated. In projects saved on a Mac, characters outside ASCII are Mac Roman: c6 is ∆, as in est2∆. The encoding of projects saved on Windows is not known; read_spf() and read_spf_contigs() decode all text as Mac Roman.

Records and blocks start with a 6-byte tag: a class byte, a version byte of 30, 31 or 32, and 00 00 00 01. In object tables and member lists the class byte has bit 02 set when the version byte is 30 (92, d2) and clear otherwise (90, d0). Both forms can occur in one file.

Read records

Each imported trace has one record that starts with the 10 bytes c0 31 00 00 00 01 63 43 72 6d (the last four spell cCrm), or with 32 in place of 31. The layout that follows is the same in both. Records that start with c2 instead appear to be reads deleted from the project: their block tables point at space that has since been reused, and they are skipped. Deleted reads can also keep the c0 tag; see "Deleted records" below. read_spf() finds reads by searching for these tags. Relative to the start of the tag:

OffsetSizeContents
444offset of the read's name, the file name it was imported under
484length of the name, including the terminating null
25964block table: 8 pairs of (offset, length), 4 bytes each

The block table lists, in order:

SlotContentsLength field
1base callsnumber of bases
2quality scores; offset and length are 0 if the read has nonenumber of bases
3unused; offset and length are 0
4peak positions, a DnFx blockcompressed size
5–8A, C, G and T trace channels, DnFx blockscompressed size

The name shown in Sequencher can differ from the original file name: reads can be renamed after import, and the record keeps only the current name.

Base calls and quality scores

Base calls take one byte each, holding a 4-bit mask with A = 1, C = 2, G = 4 and T = 8. Ambiguity codes are the sums of these (for example R = A + G = 5), and N is 15. read_spf() maps the masks to IUPAC letters and maps 0 to -. In the published projects, the two bases of a two-base code are the two strongest trace channels at that peak for 105 of 117 calls. These are the calls as edited in Sequencher, so they can differ from the original file where bases were inserted, deleted or changed.

Quality scores take one byte each and are the original Phred scores.

DnFx blocks

Peak positions and trace channels are stored as compressed series of 16-bit integers. Each block starts with a 24-byte header:

OffsetSizeContents
04the ASCII tag DnFx
44uncompressed size in bytes, two per value
84size of the payload that follows the header
124unknown; varies between blocks, possibly a checksum
16448 b7 ff bf for peak positions, 68 b7 ff bf for traces
2010
211order k of the difference predictor, 2 for peaks and 3–5 for traces
2220

The payload starts with a chunk index:

  • bytes 0–1: the number of complete 256-value chunks, floor(n / 256);

  • bytes 2–3: 01 00 in every block seen;

  • one 14-byte entry per chunk, holding the last five values of the chunk as 16-bit integers, a flag byte (0x80 or 0x00, meaning unknown) and a 3-byte position in the residual stream counted in nibbles.

The index allows random access into a long trace. read_spf() does not need it, because the residual stream that follows the index decodes from start to finish without breaks at chunk boundaries.

Predictor

Each value is predicted from the k values before it by a k-th order difference: for k = 2 the prediction is 2 * x[i - 1] - x[i - 2], and in general it is the sum over j = 1, ..., k of (-1)^(j + 1) * choose(k, j) * x[i - j]. Values before the start of the series count as 0. The stream stores the residual, the value minus its prediction, so the series is recovered by summing the residuals cumulatively k times.

Residual coding

The residual stream is read four bits at a time, high nibble first.

  • A nibble from 0 to 7 or from 9 to f is a residual from -7 to 7, read as a signed 4-bit integer.

  • The nibble 8 switches to bytes for one or more residuals. In each byte the top bit is set on the last residual of the run, after which the stream returns to nibbles. The low seven bits are a signed integer s, which stands for a residual of s + 7 if s > 0 and s - 7 if s < 0.

  • If s = 0, the next four nibbles hold a signed 16-bit integer S, which stands for S + 7 or S - 7 in the same way. Large residuals at the start of a series are stored this way.

For example, 3 d 0 7 is the residuals 3, -3, 0 and 7; 8 81 is 8 and 8 ff is -8; 8 7e 06 fb is the run -9, 13, -12.

Object IDs

Records refer to one another by 32-bit object ID rather than by offset. Object tables are tagged 92 or 90, then hold a 16-bit count and that many pairs of (file offset, ID). Pages of member IDs (below) share the 90 tag; read_spf_contigs() takes a block as an object table only if every offset in it starts a record. Some IDs that records refer to are missing from the tables as counted, but their (offset, ID) pairs still occur in the file; read_spf_contigs() finds them by searching for the ID directly after an offset that starts a record.

Contigs

Contig records start with c0 31 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00, or with 32 in place of 31. Relative to the start of the record:

OffsetSizeContents
281record type: 2 for a contig, 4 for a placement record
481number of members
494offset of the member list
534unknown; 11 in every contig seen
718offset and length of the consensus block
2058offset and length of the contig's name, null-terminated

A member list tagged d2 or d0 holds a 16-bit count and one 4-byte object ID per member. A list tagged 52 or 50 is paged: its count is the number of pages, followed by the file offset of each page, and each page is a block tagged 92 or 90 with a count and up to 32 member IDs. Records of type 0 use the same layout; in some projects one of them, named after the project file, lists the contigs.

Each member is a placement record, which holds the object ID of its read or reference sequence at offset 79. Reference sequences (records tagged cBAS, two bases per byte) have no name of their own; the placement record gives it at offset 205.

The consensus block holds one byte per alignment column. The low four bits are the base mask used for reads, and 0 where the column has no consensus base; the meaning of the high four bits is unknown. It is the consensus as last saved, not one recomputed from the reads. In the Sequencher 5.4 project, every contig held only reads of the accession it was named after, plus the reference. In the 14 published projects, every read that is not deleted belongs to a contig, and each contig's member count at offset 48 matches its member list. A contig record that starts with c2, like the deleted reads, had no live reads and is skipped.

Deleted records

Sequencher can leave the records of deleted reads and contigs in the file, with their c0 tags and data intact. read_spf() and read_spf_contigs() count a record as deleted when no object table lists it, and return such records only with deleted = TRUE. In 14 of the 16 projects examined, an object table lists every read. One published project lists all but one, and the unlisted read has the same traces as a listed one, so it is an old copy. The last project lists 4 of its 30 reads. The other 26 decode cleanly; 24 carry names from a 2011 sequencing plate, and two have names overwritten by later data. read_spf() names such reads unnamed_read_<n>.

Not yet decoded

The position, orientation and gapped sequence of each read within its contig, which the placement records also hold; annotation records (tagged c2 31 00 00) such as the end trimming applied by Sequencher; and import records tagged <ID:.
